sources.title: The Geologic Enhanced Mapping System (GEMS) Prize Challenge
sources.publisher: DrivenData, for the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Geothermal, with support from the National Lab of the Rockies
sources.facts_used: competition 306 is the GEMS Prize Challenge; total prize pool $300,000 (initial round $50,000, final round $250,000); competition end date Dec 3 2026 23:59 UTC; the submission workflow is: enrol via Compete!, download data from the data tab, make a prediction matching the submission format, click Submit then Make new submission; external data is encouraged provided it is licensed and shareable with the organisers for independent verification; the private test set is a newly expert-labeled set of faults inside the GeoDAWN region and there is spatial overlap with the training set

sources.citation: U.S. Department of Energy, Geologic Enhanced Mapping System (GEMS) Prize Official Rules, September 2026, administered by the National Laboratory of the Rockies
sources.facts_used: a submission is a single GeoTIFF with a single raster layer at 100 m resolution covering the whole GeoDAWN study area; the scoring metric is the distance-weighted Tversky index; at most three submissions per week; one final submission must be chosen for both prize rounds and must be chosen without knowledge of private-test scores; round 1 scores on a private test dataset, round 2 on an updated test dataset created by geology experts after the competition closes; the training labels come from the INGENIOUS project's Great Basin Regional Dataset Compilation (Ayling et al. 2022, DOI 10.15121/1881483) and the test labels additionally include newly identified faults labelled by experts at NLR and USGS; use of generative AI must be disclosed in the submission narrative

sources.citation: Parker, R.L., 1973, The rapid calculation of potential anomalies, Geophysical Journal International, v. 31, p. 447-455
sources.facts_used: the Fourier-series forward operator that turns an undulating interface with a constant density contrast into a gravity anomaly; the series is truncated at the point where the term amplitude falls below a tolerance, which is the criterion our forward operator implements

sources.citation: Oldenburg, D.W., 1974, The inversion and interpretation of gravity anomalies, Geophysics, v. 39, no. 4, p. 526-536
sources.facts_used: the iterative rearrangement of Parker's series that recovers interface relief from the anomaly, with a low-pass cosine taper to control the exponential growth of the high-wavenumber terms; the taper is characterised by its plateau and roll-off wavenumbers (our plateau_fraction and cutoff_wavelength)

sources.citation: Blakely, R.J., and Jachens, R.C., 1991, Regional study of mineral resources in Nevada: Insights from three-dimensional analysis of gravity and magnetic anomalies, Geological Society of America Bulletin, v. 103, no. 6, p. 795-803
sources.facts_used: isostatic residual gravity over Nevada interpreted in terms of the pre-Tertiary basement surface; this is the published precedent for reading the isostatic gravity field as a buried basement-topography product rather than as a raw channel

sources.citation: Jachens, R.C., and Moring, B.C., 1990, Maps of the thickness of Cenozoic deposits and the isostatic residual gravity over basement for Nevada, U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 90-404
sources.facts_used: Jachens & Moring's gravity/basin-depth methodology is part of the historical provenance of the organizer's gravity and depth products. Current H61U candidate construction uses band 13 alone and does not consume organizer band 15.

sources.citation: Hildenbrand, T.G., Langenheim, V.E., Mankinen, E.A., and McKee, E.H., 1999, Gravity of the Pahute Mesa-Oasis Valley region, Nye County, Nevada, U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 99-49
sources.facts_used: isostatic residual gravity inverted with the Jachens & Moring (1990) method as modified to include drill-hole data; discrete fill-density profile 1900 / 2100 / 2300 / 2450 kg/m3 over the depth intervals 0-200 / 200-600 / 600-1200 / >1200 m; pre-Tertiary basement density 2670 kg/m3 (2650-2670 commonly used); reduction density 2400 kg/m3; fill density rises to about 2450 kg/m3 by 1-2 km depth; alternative density-depth functions shift the mean basement depth by only +0.7 to -0.5 km; an 800 m reduction-density error can bias depth by about 1000 m; welded tuffs and dense volcanic domes can be mis-read as shallow basement

sources.citation: Saltus, R.W., and Jachens, R.C., 1995, Gravity and basin-depth maps of the Basin and Range Province, western United States, USGS Geophysical Investigations Map GP-1012; NOAA/NCEI distributes an official regional br_depth.xyz grid.
sources.verification: USGS publication page and partial NOAA/NCEI grid header checked; complete grid not locally obtained or calibrated.
sources.facts_used: GP-1012 is the sole permitted depth-scale calibration reference, not a prediction feature. NOAA/NCEI's br_depth.xyz header excerpt reports a 596 x 504 grid at 2 km spacing, in km, with missing value 9999; no geodetic datum was identified in the excerpt. The complete file is not present locally, so no calibration is claimed.
